body_markdown:
What draws car people to wagons, anyway? Maybe their long roofs help the lines flow and makes them look lower and sleeker. Maybe they allude to long road trips and exploration. Maybe it’s just the added utility. We’re not exactly sure why, but wagons tend to be cooler than sedans. Well, at least the right wagons are, and we’re thinking a lot about wagons and long drives on this Thanksgiving week, the busiest travel week of the year in the United States. Here are some of our favorite American wagons, powered by a good-old-fashioned V-8, listed in chronological order. Some are cheap and some are expensive, but they’re all something we’d be happy to take on a trip.


## 1957 Pontiac Star Chief Custom Safari


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


**347cid/317hp Tri-Power**


[Median #2 (excellent) Value: $70,200](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/pontiac/star_chief/1957/1957-pontiac-star_chief-custom_safari?id=aCn1I000000DTlcSAG&condition=excellent)


The Tri-Five Chevy gets all the songs and the glory, but Pontiac was alongside the whole way, even getting a version of the[Nomad](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1957+chevrolet+nomad) called the Safari. Its fantastic two-door wagon profile, with its slanted B-pillar and canted forward tailgate, looked good with the chrome trim of the 1955 and 1956 models. The 1957 Safari, however, took things to the perfect amount of excess. The chrome trim is perfect. With its triple-carbed, 347-cubic-inch, 317hp V-8, it also outpowered even the fuel-injected 283 available in the Nomad. The Star Chief-based Custom Safari is also generally a bit cheaper than its better-known Chevy sibling.


## 1969 Buick Sportwagon


Hagerty Marketplace | David Ross


Paul Stenquist


**350cid/230hp**


[Median #2 (excellent) Value: $17,800](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/sportwagon/1969/1969-buick-sportwagon-base?id=aCn1I000000DK54SAG&condition=excellent)


Just like the Safari is the lesser-known sibling of the Nomad, the Buick Sportwagon is the often-forgotten twin of the[Oldsmobile Vista Cruiser](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/oldsmobile/vista_cruiser/1969/1969-oldsmobile-vista_cruiser-base?id=aCn1I000000D2Q8SAK) . Both feature fantastic rooflines with additional, roof-mounted windows for better road-trip sightseeing from the rear seats. We picked the Sportwagon because we’re suckers for Buick Ventiports and Sweepspears. The Sportwagon came with the two-barrel version of the 350 V-8, which meant a lower compression ratio. That extra compression and better breathing was good for 50 horsepower, but required higher-octane fuel. For wide-open roads and cross-country mileage, the cruiser engine suits this wagon fine, not that we’d shun a period-correct[GS 400](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/gs_400/1969/1969-buick-gs_400-base?id=aCn1I000000CsnZSAS) engine swap.


## 1970 Ford Torino Squire


Ford


**429cid/360hp**


**[Median #2 (excellent) Value: $30,300](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/torino/1970/1970-ford-torino-base?id=aCn1I000000DTRsSAO&condition=excellent)**


The[1970 Torino](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/torino/1970/1970-ford-torino-gt?id=aCn1I000000DMgpSAG) is one of the most underrated muscle cars of its time. Ford nailed it with the styling, particularly the aggressive front end with its tucked-in chrome bumper and optional hidden headlights. The design also translated particularly well into the four-door wagon. Just imagine the wood-clad longroof pictured above with an angry 429 under the hood. When people talk about “sleepers,” they mean cars like this. The 351 small-block was no slouch either with 300hp (and a #2 value of $28K), and we wouldn’t blame you for picking up one of those either, especially if cross-country road trips were on the agenda.


## 1991–96 Buick Roadmaster


Cameron Neveu


**350cid/260hp**


**[Median #2 (Excellent) Value: $32,500](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/roadmaster/1996/1996-buick-roadmaster-estate_wagon?id=aCn1I000000DJ0uSAG&condition=excellent)**


We’re pricking the Buick wagon over its[Chevy Caprice](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/caprice_classic/1993/1993-chevrolet-caprice_classic-base?id=aCn1I000000CzlaSAC) counterpart because although both wagons are very similar, the Roadmaster came with the Vista Roof for improved sightseeing. Chevrolet also offered two 4.3-liter engines, a V-6 and a V-8, while the Roadmaster was V-8 only. The 350-cubic-inch LT1 was similar to the sportier version found in the Corvette, Firebird, and Camaro, but used iron cylinder heads rather than aluminum. Still, for the early ’90s they offered solid performance even if burdened by the bulk of a B-body. These wagons saw serious family truckster duty and racked up the miles. As such, there’s a big divide between the value of a #3 (good) and a #2 (excellent) example, with the later being more than three times as valuable.


## 2005–08 Dodge Magnum SRT-8


FCA


**6.1L/425hp**


**[Median #2 (excellent) Value: $36,300](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/dodge/magnum_(truck)/2008/2008-dodge-magnum_(truck)-srt~8?id=aCn1I000000DA3rSAG&condition=excellent)**


As Dodge’s wagon counterpart to its Charger sedan in the 2000s, the Magnum received the same powerplants. For V-8s, that meant the 345hp 5.7-liter Hemi in the R/T and the 425hp 6.1-liter for the SRT-8, both channeling power trough a five-speed automatic. We like the SRT-8’s imposing style, with the stockier crosshair grille and squared-off front making a good match for the heavier wagon profile. Unfortunately, the burly wagon didn’t survive long enough to get the much-improved interior refresh that the Charger benefitted from in 2011, or the 707hp Hellcat V-8 in 2015.


## 2011-2015 Cadillac CTS-V


Cadillac


**6.2L/556hp**


**[Median #2 (excellent) Value: $88,000](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/cadillac/cts~v/2013/2013-cadillac-cts~v-base?id=aCn1I000000Cyp3SAC&condition=excellent)**


We’d be willing to put up with a lot compromises for a 556hp supercharged LSA V-8 and an optional six-speed manual transmission, but the CTS-V wagon also looks and drives like a dream. The bad news is that Cadillac only built about 1800 of them. Worse news is that only around 500 getting the manual. The looks, performance, and rarity have all combined to make this one of the hottest wagons on the market, with values for #1 (concours, or best in the world) examples managing to crack six figures. Subtract 15% for any CTS-V wagons fitted with the automatic that, to be honest, still works just fine for fast wagon duty.
